what_we_value: Management Science would value the field experiments run with a real platform and the counterintuitive finding that a governance tool can backfire when power between the two sides is unequal, but it would ask whether the mechanism has been pinned down and whether the result says something general about platform design beyond stated reactions to a proposed system.

suggestions.direction: Build a simple formal model of how a platform adopts a rating system when the two sides differ in power and outside options. Derive predictions about when the system raises or lowers participation on each side, and test those predictions against how responses vary across employer income and worker characteristics.
suggestions.why: Management Science rewards empirical work tied to a tractable model that explains a counterintuitive result and generates predictions that can be checked.

suggestions.direction: Use additional treatment arms or survey measures to separate competing mechanisms on the worker side: fear of retaliatory ratings, loss of bargaining power, privacy and reputation concerns, and distrust of the platform. Do the same on the employer side for anticipated worker exit versus status concerns.
suggestions.why: Reviewers will want to know why the backfire happens, and identifying the mechanism turns a single setting into a lesson about platform governance in general.

suggestions.direction: Look beyond stated reactions and immediate disengagement to longer-term behavioral outcomes such as matches, applications, and retention. Then test design variants (one-sided versus two-sided ratings, anonymity, delayed disclosure) that could reduce the backfire.
suggestions.why: A design recommendation backed by real behavioral outcomes is the kind of managerial contribution this journal looks for.

revised_abstract: Rating systems are a common governance tool on two-sided platforms, and they are usually assumed to benefit both sides through indirect network effects. We argue that when there is a large power gap between the two sides, the rated side may oppose ratings, and the rating side may anticipate that opposition. We develop a model of how a platform adopts a rating system under unequal power between the sides, which predicts when participation falls on each side. We test the model with two field experiments on a Singapore labor platform that matches foreign domestic workers with employer families. On average, employers were indifferent to the proposed system, even when its benefits to them were highlighted, and the highest-income employers responded negatively. Workers who were informed of the system disengaged from the platform completely. Planned treatment arms will separate competing mechanisms (fear of retaliation, loss of bargaining power, and distrust of the platform), and planned analyses will track downstream matching and retention. We also plan to evaluate design variants, including anonymity and two-sided ratings, to identify conditions under which rating systems can be introduced without driving the weaker side away. The results inform platform governance and design.

what_we_value: We value the theoretical move from static stereotyping to stereotypes updated through experience, from individuals to gender categories, and the rare longitudinal hiring data. We would question whether positive interactions really reduce stereotypes, rather than reflecting match quality, selection, or reputation signals on the platform, and whether the paper adds organizational theory beyond the labor economics of discrimination.

suggestions.direction: Theorize and test category-level updating as an organizational learning process. Compare positive with negative interactions (looking for asymmetry or loss aversion), and test whether updating fades over time or across job types.
suggestions.why: Linking stereotype revision to experiential and vicarious learning theory would connect the paper to a core Organization Science conversation, instead of standing only as a discrimination finding.

suggestions.direction: Strengthen identification of the mechanism. Use variation in how uncertain a job is (for example, task verifiability, contract type, or the availability of platform reputation signals) to show that trustworthiness inferences drive the effects.
suggestions.why: Reviewers will need to see that stereotype updating explains the results better than match quality or simple information effects.

suggestions.direction: Examine how employer characteristics and the platform's design for reputation and ratings moderate whether interactions generalize from individuals to gender categories.
suggestions.why: This would show how organizational and market structures shape inequality, a theme this community values, and would point to design implications.

revised_abstract: Employers in online labor marketplaces often prefer women over men because of stereotypes that women are more trustworthy. These stereotypes are salient where transactions are uncertain. We theorize hiring as an experiential learning process: employers' interactions with individual workers revise their stereotypes about those individuals and about gender categories. We use rare large-scale, longitudinal hiring data from an online labor marketplace and estimate linear probability models with job fixed effects. We find that employers prefer to rehire workers with whom they had positive interactions, and that men benefit more than women from these interactions, consistent with weakened negative stereotypes about men's trustworthiness. Employers also prefer new workers of the same gender as workers they had positive experiences with, so learning extends from individuals to categories. Planned analyses will compare positive with negative interactions to test for asymmetric updating. They will also test whether the effects are stronger in jobs that are more uncertain and less verifiable, and whether platform reputation signals and employer experience moderate how far learning generalizes. These analyses will explain how market structures shape when experience reproduces or erodes gender inequality.

what_we_value: SMJ would value the large-scale longitudinal hiring data and the evidence that experience updates stereotypes, but would ask what the strategic contribution is: how do firms' hiring choices shape their access to human capital, their performance, or their competitive position, beyond what a labor or organizational-behavior audience already studies?

suggestions.direction: Frame the work through strategic human capital and market frictions: treat trustworthiness stereotypes as an information friction, and interactions as private information that lets employers find undervalued talent (here, men).
suggestions.why: SMJ rewards work that ties labor-market frictions to how firms acquire and capture value from human capital (e.g., IFRS/gender gap, NFL frictions).

suggestions.direction: Connect hiring decisions to employer outcomes, such as project quality, cost, completion, and rehiring efficiency, to test whether experience-based updating creates performance advantages or locks employers in.
suggestions.why: Showing performance consequences turns a story about bias into a story about firm strategy and competitive advantage.

suggestions.direction: Strengthen identification using quasi-exogenous variation in first interactions (e.g., platform-assigned matches or random worker unavailability) and test mechanisms with heterogeneity by transaction uncertainty and platform reputation signals.
suggestions.why: SMJ reviewers expect causal designs and clear mechanisms, and generalization by category (same-gender hiring) is open to selection concerns as the evidence stands.

revised_abstract: Strategic human capital research holds that labor-market frictions shape which firms can access and capture value from talent. We argue that gender stereotypes about trustworthiness act as such a friction in online labor markets, where transactions are uncertain, and that firsthand interactions give employers private information that can override the stereotypes. Using large-scale longitudinal hiring data from an online labor marketplace and linear probability models with job fixed effects, we find that employers prefer to rehire workers with whom they had positive interactions. Men, who face less favorable trustworthiness stereotypes, benefit more from these interactions. Employers also become more likely to hire unknown workers of the same gender as their positive prior hires, which suggests that experience with individuals updates beliefs about gender categories. We plan analyses that exploit quasi-exogenous variation in first matches to strengthen causal inference, examine whether effects vary with transaction uncertainty, and test whether experience-based updating improves employer outcomes such as project quality and cost. Our findings would show how employers' learning reshapes their access to undervalued human capital.

what_we_value: We value large-scale behavioral data on how employers update beliefs about social categories, which builds on work in this journal such as the loss-aversion study of hiring by country, but we question whether linear probability models with job fixed effects can separate stereotype updating from worker quality, sorting, and mechanical rehiring, and whether the contribution goes beyond confirming that experience reduces reliance on stereotypes.

suggestions.direction: Find plausibly exogenous variation in interaction quality or worker gender, such as feedback shocks, quasi-random worker availability, platform design changes, or a field experiment that randomizes gender signals on profiles.
suggestions.why: Management Science reviewers will expect causal identification that rules out unobserved worker quality and employer selection, not just correlations with fixed effects.

suggestions.direction: Build a simple Bayesian learning model, perhaps with asymmetric updating, that predicts how strongly employers update from positive versus negative experiences by gender, and when experience generalizes from an individual to a gender category. Then test those predictions, including negative interactions and how similar the jobs are.
suggestions.why: Formal predictions with sharp tests turn a descriptive pattern into a contribution about belief formation, which fits the journal's strong theory-plus-evidence approach.

suggestions.direction: Measure the consequences for workers and the platform: earnings gaps, how long women's hiring advantage lasts, and platform design options (for example, reputation systems that reduce reliance on stereotypes).
suggestions.why: Showing managerial and platform-design implications broadens the paper's audience beyond the sociology of gender to operations and platform-strategy readers.

revised_abstract: In online labor markets, employers favor women workers, a pattern often attributed to stereotypes that women are more trustworthy when transactions are uncertain. We study how direct experience changes such category-based beliefs. We develop a Bayesian learning framework that predicts (i) that individual interactions reduce reliance on gender stereotypes, more so for the group stereotyped as less trustworthy, and (ii) that experiences with individuals spill over into beliefs about gender categories, depending on how similar the jobs are. Using large-scale, longitudinal hiring data from an online labor marketplace, we find that employers prefer rehiring workers with whom they had positive interactions, that men gain more than women from these interactions, and that employers subsequently favor unknown workers of the same gender as their prior positive hires. We plan to strengthen identification using quasi-exogenous variation in worker availability and feedback, to examine negative interactions and asymmetric updating, and to quantify the effects on gender earnings gaps. Our results show how platform reputation systems and repeated interactions shape whether stereotypes persist in digital hiring.

what_we_value: We would value the chance to see the whole distribution of firm growth, including stagnant and shrinking firms, at population scale, but as written this is a data resource aimed at strategic management, not a theory-building contribution about organizations, and we would ask what organizational mechanism the dataset helps explain.

suggestions.direction: Build the paper around one theoretical puzzle, such as why stagnant firms persist and fewer young firms reach high growth. Draw on organizational ecology, inertia, or a behavioral theory of the firm to explain this, and test predictions derived from that theory with the BDS-HG distributions.
suggestions.why: Organization Science publishes papers that advance organization theory; a dataset alone is not enough.

suggestions.direction: Link the BDS-HG cells to organizational-level data in the restricted Census data, such as LBD establishment structure, multi-unit status, or ownership changes. Use this to test whether organizational form and structure explain how firms move between high-growth, stagnant, and shrinking states.
suggestions.why: Mechanisms at the level of organizations are what this journal's readers expect, rather than descriptions of aggregate trends.

suggestions.direction: Treat stagnation as a distinct organizational state, not just a residual category. Theorize how firms enter and leave it, and how this depends on firm age and on the competitive environment.
suggestions.why: Calling stagnation a phenomenon that existing growth and learning theories have overlooked gives the paper a conceptual contribution that fits the journal.

revised_abstract: Theories of organizational growth focus mostly on the winners and treat firms that stagnate or shrink as residual cases. We argue that stagnation is a distinct organizational state with its own dynamics. Drawing on theories of organizational inertia and the liability of newness, we theorize how firm age, size, and multi-unit structure shape the chances that a firm enters, remains in, or leaves high-growth, stagnant, and shrinking states. To test these ideas, we construct a new public-use dataset from US Census Bureau administrative records, Business Dynamics Statistics—High Growth (BDS-HG). It covers the full distribution of firm growth from 1978 to 2021, broken down by firm age, size, industry, and region. Descriptively, the share of high-growth firms has declined, especially among young and small firms, while the share of stagnant firms has risen. We plan to link BDS-HG to firm-level Census data to estimate how firms move between growth states and to examine whether organizational structure and competitive environments help explain why stagnation persists. We discuss what this means for theories of organizational growth, adaptation, and selection, and how researchers can use BDS-HG to benchmark how well their samples generalize.

what_we_value: SMJ values data resources that help strategy research build cumulative knowledge, as its replication and methods pieces show, but the board will ask what this dataset teaches us about firm strategy and competitive advantage, beyond a descriptive account of US business dynamics.

suggestions.direction: Build the paper around a strategy question, such as whether the fall in high-growth firms and the rise in stagnant firms reflect more persistent incumbent advantage, more industry concentration, or weaker entry, and test this using industry-by-age-by-size variation.
suggestions.why: SMJ publishes work that advances theory on why firm performance differs, so the descriptive trends need to be linked to resource-based or competitive-dynamics explanations.

suggestions.direction: Turn the benchmarking idea into a method: show how common strategy samples (e.g., Compustat, VC-backed startups, Crunchbase) compare with the full BDS-HG growth distribution, and show how reweighting changes published estimates.
suggestions.why: Representativeness and generalizability are central concerns in SMJ's replication and methods conversations, so a demonstrated correction tool would make the contribution concrete.

suggestions.direction: Replace the three loosely connected applications with one or two deep applications tied to active SMJ debates, such as entrepreneurial strategy and scaling, or the persistence of firm performance.
suggestions.why: Focused applications show the dataset's theoretical value better than a broad tour of uses.

revised_abstract: Strategy research on firm growth and performance heterogeneity often relies on selected samples (public firms, venture-backed startups) whose representativeness is unknown. Using US Census Bureau administrative data, we introduce Business Dynamics Statistics—High Growth (BDS-HG), a public-use dataset that captures the full firm growth distribution from 1978 to 2021, including high-growth, stagnant, and shrinking firms, by firm age, size, industry, region, and year. We document a decline in the share of high-growth firms, especially among young and small firms, and a rise in stagnant firms. We then ask whether these shifts are consistent with growing incumbent advantage or with weakening scaling among new entrants. We plan to examine this by relating changes in the growth distribution to industry concentration and the persistence of firm performance. Second, we propose a benchmarking procedure that compares widely used strategy samples with the population growth distribution. We plan to illustrate how reweighting may change inferences from published studies. BDS-HG offers strategy scholars a foundation for theory-relevant research on growth, stagnation, and generalizability.

what_we_value: We value the Census data and how much of the growth distribution it covers, but this journal publishes papers that identify a mechanism behind firm growth or test a theory about it, and a paper that mainly introduces a dataset and describes its trends, written for strategy researchers, doesn't count as a contribution here.

suggestions.direction: Shift the paper's main question from introducing the dataset to explaining one result: why high-growth firms became less common and stagnant firms more common. Test competing explanations against each other, for example incumbent concentration, intangible capital, and limits on how easily resources move between firms, using variation across industries, regions, and cohorts.
suggestions.why: Papers in Management Science need an answer to a causal or theoretical question; documenting trends alone is not enough.

suggestions.direction: Use a quasi-experimental shock, such as state noncompete reforms, changes in bank deregulation, or China import competition, to estimate how policy or market frictions shift where firms fall across the high-growth, stagnant and shrinking categories.
suggestions.why: The journal rewards credible identification, and the strength of BDS-HG is that it covers the whole growth distribution, so it can show effects that a sample of only high-growth firms would miss.

suggestions.direction: Build a short formal model or a set of decomposition results linking how firms select into growth categories, how they learn, and how resources are reallocated, and use the BDS-HG patterns to test the model's predictions.
suggestions.why: Pairing a model with large-scale evidence matches the kind of contribution this journal values and makes the paper about more than the data.

revised_abstract: Why has US business dynamism declined? Using Census Bureau administrative data from 1978 to 2021, we build BDS-HG, a public dataset that covers the full distribution of firm growth: high-growth, stagnant and shrinking firms, broken down by firm age, size, industry, region and year. We document a decline in the share of high-growth firms, concentrated among young and small firms, and a rise in the share of stagnant firms. We then examine what drives these shifts. We develop a simple framework in which frictions that limit the reallocation of resources move firms from the high-growth tail into stagnation, and we derive predictions that separate this channel from rising concentration among incumbents and from the growth of intangible capital. We plan to test these predictions using staggered state-level policy changes, including noncompete enforcement and banking deregulation, together with differences in exposure across industries, in difference-in-differences designs that estimate effects on each part of the growth distribution. We also show how researchers can use BDS-HG to check how representative their samples are. The results will inform managers and policymakers about the conditions that allow firms to scale.

what_we_value: The question of how GAI changes the direction of innovation, and not just its pace, matters to us, but as written the paper reads like a strategy or economics-of-innovation study; we would ask what it says about organizing, about who gets to innovate, and about how developers' work and identities change.

suggestions.direction: Theorize the developer-level mechanism as a change in the boundaries of who can innovate and how work is divided between ideation and implementation. Separate newcomers who enter because GAI lowers the implementation barrier from incumbents who reallocate their effort, and test each group on its own.
suggestions.why: Organization Science values theory about how technology reshapes work and expertise (e.g., AI augmentation, occupational boundaries), and a clear account of who does what would make that contribution visible.

suggestions.direction: Add qualitative evidence, such as developer interviews or the content of forums and changelogs, to show how developers actually use GAI in ideation versus implementation and why they move away from building on prior generations.
suggestions.why: A mixed-methods design that shows the practices behind the mechanism is a common and valued template in this journal, and it would strengthen the causal story beyond inference from outcomes.

suggestions.direction: Look at collective and ecosystem consequences. Does the shift toward original but not more novel products homogenize the add-on ecosystem, crowd attention, or weaken cumulative knowledge building? Test this with planned analyses of similarity between products and of how often later products build on earlier ones.
suggestions.why: Linking individual-level change to organizational and field-level outcomes, like cumulative learning and the structure of categories, connects the paper to core conversations in Organization Science.

revised_abstract: How does generative artificial intelligence (GAI) reshape who innovates and what they create? We theorize that GAI lowers implementation barriers and supports ideation. This changes how innovative work is divided: it lets newcomers build products that were previously beyond their reach, and it lets experienced developers reallocate effort. We propose that, together, these shifts move activity away from generational innovation, which builds on prior product versions, and toward original innovation, which is new to the market but not necessarily more novel. We study browser add-on developers. Our planned analyses separate newcomer entry from incumbent reallocation, and we will add developer interviews and analyses of forum content to trace how GAI is used in ideation versus implementation. We also plan to examine consequences at the level of the ecosystem: how similar products are to one another, and whether later products continue to build on earlier ones. Our goal is to clarify whether GAI broadens participation at the cost of cumulative knowledge building. We contribute to research on technology and work, occupational boundaries, and the organization of innovation.

what_we_value: We value a timely, well-identified look at how GAI changes the direction of innovation, not just how much of it happens. We would question whether "generational vs. original" innovation is a strategic outcome, meaning one that affects competitive positioning, value capture, or firm-level heterogeneity, or whether it is mainly a product-development outcome that belongs in an IS or innovation journal.

suggestions.direction: Connect the shift in innovation direction to competitive consequences: entry into new niches vs. crowded product spaces, differentiation from incumbents, survival, and user adoption or value capture.
suggestions.why: SMJ papers need to show performance or competitive-advantage implications, not only changes in what innovators do.

suggestions.direction: Theorize and test heterogeneity across developers' resources and capabilities (prior experience, team vs. solo, company-backed vs. independent), and separate the two mechanisms: capability expansion through new entrants and effort reallocation by incumbents.
suggestions.why: Grounding the mechanisms in resource- and capability-based arguments ties the work to core strategy theory and explains which developers gain.

suggestions.direction: Strengthen causal identification by exploiting staggered GAI access or exposure, such as language- or API-specific coding-assistant coverage, in a difference-in-differences design with clear construct validation of original vs. generational innovation.
suggestions.why: SMJ reviewers expect credible quasi-experimental designs, and so far these claims rest on new constructs that need validating.

revised_abstract: How does generative artificial intelligence (GAI) change the direction of innovation, and who benefits competitively? Drawing on resource- and capability-based perspectives, we argue that GAI lowers barriers in both ideation and implementation. This lets resource-constrained developers create products previously beyond their reach, and lets experienced developers reallocate effort away from generational innovation (improving existing products) toward original innovation (products new to the market). We study browser add-ons and use differences in how much GAI coding assistance was available across programming contexts to build a difference-in-differences design. We validate measures of original and generational innovation using text-based product similarity. Planned analyses separate capability expansion among new entrants from effort reallocation among incumbent developers, and test how effects vary with developer experience, team structure, and organizational backing. We then examine competitive consequences: whether GAI-enabled original products enter less crowded niches, achieve greater differentiation, and attain higher adoption and survival. The study aims to explain how a general-purpose technology reshapes the basis of competitive heterogeneity among innovators, with implications for strategy research on AI, entry, and innovation direction.

what_we_value: Management Science would value a well-identified, quantified causal account of how generative AI changes the direction of innovation, as opposed to just its volume, but it would question whether the browser add-on evidence separates a GAI effect from secular trends, and whether "generational" versus "original" innovation is measured precisely and validated.

suggestions.direction: Anchor identification in an exogenous shock to GAI access, such as the ChatGPT/Copilot release timing, regional or language availability restrictions, or a developer-level difference-in-differences comparing developers whose language or tooling GAI covers with those it does not.
suggestions.why: The journal expects credible causal estimates with effect sizes, and right now the abstract offers only 'empirical evidence for these arguments.'

suggestions.direction: Build and validate a text- and code-based measure of novelty and generational versus original innovation, for example embedding distance from prior add-ons and from earlier versions of the same product, and report market outcomes such as installs and ratings.
suggestions.why: Precise new measures that link the direction of innovation to performance are what turn a plausible story into a contribution here, in the way published papers on startup differentiation and destabilization indexes did.

suggestions.direction: Separate the two proposed mechanisms, entry by developers newly able to build products versus reallocation of effort by incumbents, through heterogeneity by prior developer skill and task (ideation versus implementation), and ideally formalize this in a simple model of the task-cost trade-off.
suggestions.why: The journal rewards papers that clearly separate mechanisms and connect them to theory, which also supports the claim that the findings generalize to other domains.

revised_abstract: How does generative AI (GAI) change the direction of innovation, beyond its volume? We develop a simple task-based framework. In it, GAI lowers the costs of ideation and implementation, which (i) lets new developers bring products to market that were previously out of their reach and (ii) leads existing developers to reallocate effort away from generational innovation (new versions of their own products) and toward original innovation (new-to-market products that are not necessarily more novel). We test these predictions with data on browser add-on products. For identification, we use a difference-in-differences design based on the staggered availability of GAI tools and on differences in how well GAI supports different programming tasks and languages. We build and validate text- and code-embedding measures of novelty relative to the market and to each product's own prior versions, and we relate them to installs and ratings. We plan analyses of heterogeneity by prior developer skill to separate the entry mechanism from the reallocation mechanism. We discuss implications for innovation strategy, the management of developer ecosystems, and whether the findings generalize to other domains.

what_we_value: Organization Science would value the credible causal evidence on how buyers govern their suppliers, but it would question whether the paper builds organizational theory about relationships, power and interorganizational governance, or whether it mainly evaluates a policy, which reads more like a strategy or operations journal.

suggestions.direction: Recast the study as a theory of interorganizational governance. Show how the shadow of exit (the threat to end the relationship) works together with relational embeddedness and dependence, and develop hypotheses from relational contracting and resource dependence about why both competition and long relationships strengthen the threat.
suggestions.why: The journal rewards mechanisms that resolve a theoretical tension, and here the tension is between relational and coercive views of governance, not a test of which tool works best.

suggestions.direction: Add qualitative evidence from buyer compliance staff and supplier managers to show how suppliers interpret threats, whether they make real changes or just decouple, and how they respond organizationally.
suggestions.why: Organization Science values mixed methods that open the black box, and decoupling is a central concern in its private-regulation research.

suggestions.direction: Test whether the improvements last and are substantive. Check later audits, other dimensions such as health and safety versus wages, and whether suppliers drop out of the relationship, as planned extensions.
suggestions.why: Without these checks, a 22-point jump in pass rates could reflect gaming rather than real organizational change, and reviewers will raise that.

revised_abstract: Buyers increasingly govern the social performance of their suppliers, yet theory disagrees about whether coercive or cooperative approaches change supplier behavior. We develop a theory of the "shadow of exit." It proposes that the threat to end a relationship motivates suppliers to the extent that they depend on the buyer and value the relationship, so that coercion and relational embeddedness complement each other rather than substitute for each other. Using a regression discontinuity design on a buyer's supplier-management actions, we find that suppliers raised their probability of passing labor audits by 22 percentage points only when the action carried a threat to discontinue business. The response was strongest among suppliers facing more supply chain competition and among those in longer-term relationships with the buyer. In planned extensions, we examine whether improvements persist and extend to other dimensions of labor standards, or instead reflect decoupling. We also plan interviews with buyer and supplier managers to trace how threats are interpreted and turned into organizational change. The study contributes to research on interorganizational governance, private regulation, and the relational foundations of coercive power.

what_we_value: SMJ would value the causal identification (an RDD) of how buyers govern supplier social performance and the moderators tied to competition and relationship duration, but it would question whether the paper speaks to strategy theory (governance, relational contracting, value creation and capture) rather than only to regulatory and operations debates, and whether the buyer gets anything out of it.

suggestions.direction: Frame the study within governance theory by setting the credible threat to end the relationship (a formal, hostage-like sanction) against relational governance. Theorize when the two work as complements or substitutes, using the moderation by relationship length.
suggestions.why: SMJ rewards contributions to theories of firm boundaries and inter-firm governance, and the finding about long-term relationships speaks directly to the debate over whether relational and formal governance are complements.

suggestions.direction: Test what the threats cost and gain the buyer: whether suppliers were actually dropped, whether the buyer's sourcing volume, prices, or lead times changed, and whether supplier improvements lasted or reversed after the threat passed.
suggestions.why: The journal cares about value creation and capture, and it wants to know whether social-performance governance is costly to the buyer or durable, not just whether audit pass rates went up.

suggestions.direction: Use heterogeneity in supplier dependence and the buyer's bargaining power (the buyer's share of supplier output, how easily the supplier could switch to other buyers) to show the mechanism behind why threats work.
suggestions.why: Explaining how and why, and not only whether, a strategy works is what lifts an empirical paper to an SMJ-level theoretical contribution.

revised_abstract: A firm's social performance increasingly depends on its suppliers, yet theories of inter-firm governance disagree on whether buyers should rely on credible sanctions or on cooperative, relational approaches. We theorize that threats to end the relationship work as formal governance, and that their effect depends on the supplier's dependence on the buyer and on relational embeddedness. Using a regression discontinuity design on a buyer's actions to manage supplier labor compliance, we estimate the causal effects of governance actions with and without threatened penalties. Suppliers improved, raising their probability of passing labor audits by 22 percentage points, only when the action included a threat to discontinue business. Threats were most effective when suppliers faced more supply chain competition and had longer relationships with the buyer, which suggests that formal and relational governance complement each other. Planned analyses examine whether the effects depend on supplier dependence, whether improvements last, and what the buyer gains or loses in terms of supplier exits and sourcing outcomes. The study clarifies when sanctions help buyers create value through responsible supply chains.

what_we_value: We'd value the causal RD evidence on how buyers govern supplier labor practices, which is close in spirit to the Nike lean study we published. We'd ask whether the paper goes beyond showing that threats work, by building a mechanism-based model of when penalties pay off and by measuring outcomes that don't depend only on audits.

suggestions.direction: Build a simple formal model of buyer threats versus cooperation. It should show how supplier outside options (competition) and relationship value (shadow of the future) shape how credible a threat is and how suppliers respond. Then test the model's sharper predictions in the RD.
suggestions.why: Management Science rewards empirical papers that tie identification to a clear economic mechanism, such as relational-contract logic, rather than to an informal debate in the literature.

suggestions.direction: Look at whether improvements are real or merely gaming the audit. Use later unannounced audits, specific violation categories, persistence over time, and spillovers to other buyers' audits.
suggestions.why: Reviewers will question whether passing audits reflects real changes in labor conditions or just compliance behavior aimed at the audit.

suggestions.direction: Measure the buyer-side costs and trade-offs. These include actual terminations, order reallocation, supplier exit, and changes in prices or delivery performance, which together give a net assessment of the penalty strategy.
suggestions.why: Spelling out the operational and commercial trade-offs turns the finding into a managerial design result that the journal's audience can act on.

revised_abstract: Corporate social performance depends partly on suppliers' behavior, yet when buyers should threaten penalties rather than cooperate remains contested. We develop a model in which a threat to discontinue business works through suppliers' outside options and the value of continuing the relationship. The model predicts that threats are more effective when supply chain competition is intense and relationships are long-term. Using a regression discontinuity design based on the buyer's audit-score thresholds for remediation actions, we estimate the causal effects of typical supplier-management actions with and without threatened penalties. Suppliers raised their probability of passing labor audits by 22 percentage points only when actions included a threat to discontinue business, and responses were stronger under higher competition and longer relationships. Planned analyses examine whether improvements reflect real change or audit gaming, using unannounced audits, violation categories, and persistence over time. We also plan to assess the buyer-side consequences of threats: terminations, order reallocation, and supplier exit. The results are intended to inform how firms design supply chain governance for social performance.

what_we_value: We'd value treating the ecosystem as an organizational structure that shapes what firms choose to acquire. We'd question whether a paper about acquisition synergies, framed in strategy-economics terms, says anything about organizing: how interdependence among complementors is coordinated, how it is perceived, and how it is governed.

suggestions.direction: Recast ecosystem synergy as a problem of organizing interdependence: theorize acquisitions as a way to coordinate with third-party complementors that substitutes for or complements governance at the platform level, and connect it to the literatures on interorganizational coordination and on organizational boundaries.
suggestions.why: Organization Science rewards papers that show how organizational arrangements solve coordination problems, not papers that only list new types of synergy.

suggestions.direction: Study what happens after the acquisition: whether complementors join, leave, or re-link around the combined firm's components, and whether the predicted cluster and centrality benefits actually appear.
suggestions.why: Testing whether third parties actually respond would show the mechanism and the ecosystem-wide consequences, not just the acquirer's motive inferred from its choices.

suggestions.direction: Explain the null or weaker result for centrality and add contingencies, such as the acquirer's existing position, how mature the ecosystem is, or how modular the technology is. Also consider adding qualitative evidence on how managers perceive ecosystem structure.
suggestions.why: Boundary conditions and microfoundations of how managers notice ecosystem structure turn a descriptive pattern into a theory, which this journal's reviewers will expect.

revised_abstract: How do firms use acquisitions to organize their position among interdependent complementors? We theorize acquisitions as a boundary choice for coordinating interdependence in an ecosystem. In this view, firms absorb targets in order to reshape how their components connect with third-party complementors. We distinguish three levels of ecosystem structure: local interdependence, cluster membership, and centrality. We argue that each implies a different coordination problem, and that acquisitions can address these problems by strengthening, attracting, or bridging complementarities. We call the resulting value ecosystem synergy. Using network data on component co-use in the e-commerce technology industry, we find that firms choose targets that increase local interdependence and cluster presence, but not centrality. We use this pattern to theorize the limits of acquisition as a coordination tool. Planned analyses (1) test whether complementors re-link around the merged firm after the acquisition, (2) examine contingencies such as ecosystem maturity and modularity, and (3) use interviews to explore how managers perceive ecosystem structure. The study connects research on ecosystems with theories of organizational boundaries and interorganizational coordination.

what_we_value: We value that the paper ties ecosystem structure to corporate strategy (M&A) and proposes a new source of acquisition synergy. We would ask whether "ecosystem synergy" actually creates value, and whether network position causes target choice or just reflects unobserved strategic similarity.

suggestions.direction: Link target choice to outcomes: after a deal, measure complementor entry, multihoming, and integration with the combined firm's components, plus acquirer abnormal returns or performance, to show that ecosystem synergies are realized.
suggestions.why: Right now the paper infers synergy from what firms choose, and reviewers will want proof that this value creation actually happens.

suggestions.direction: Strengthen identification. Build matched counterfactual targets (for example, a conditional logit with control pairs drawn from targets in the same technology or market), and use plausibly exogenous shifts in ecosystem structure, such as a platform API change or a major component exit.
suggestions.why: Reviewers at this journal expect credible causal claims that separate ecosystem-structure motives from ordinary product-market relatedness and technological relatedness.

suggestions.direction: Explain why centrality was not supported, and add theoretical boundary conditions: complementor bargaining power, the risk of a platform-owner response, and whether firms are value-capture or value-creation oriented.
suggestions.why: Engaging with this null result and with value-capture theory would sharpen the contribution to ecosystem theory and to the resource-based view, beyond reporting which effects were confirmed.

revised_abstract: We examine how ecosystem structure shapes acquisition choices and outcomes. We theorize ecosystem synergy: value created when combining the acquirer's and target's ecosystem positions improves the combined firm's alignment with third-party complementors. We distinguish three levels of ecosystem structure (local interdependence, clusters, and centrality). Ecosystem synergy, we argue, arises from strengthening, attracting, or connecting complementarities, and its effects depend on complementor bargaining power and the risk of a response from the platform owner. In the e-commerce technology industry, firms acquire targets that increase the local interdependence of their components and their presence in component clusters. Centrality does not drive target choice, which we explain theoretically. To separate ecosystem motives from conventional relatedness, we plan to compare realized deals with matched counterfactual targets and to exploit exogenous shifts in ecosystem structure. We also plan to test whether these synergies materialize, measured as post-acquisition complementor entry and integration and as acquirer performance. By linking ecosystem structure to corporate strategy, the study extends theories of acquisition synergy, value creation, and value capture to settings where value depends on third parties.

what_we_value: We would value a new, measurable kind of acquisition synergy tied to how ecosystems are structured, but we would question whether the target-choice correlations identify value creation and benefits to the ecosystem, since those are claimed and not shown.

suggestions.direction: Formalize ecosystem synergy in a simple model of acquirer, target and complementors that yields sharp, testable predictions about which targets get chosen and who benefits (acquirer, target, third parties).
suggestions.why: Management Science rewards mechanisms derived from a model over frameworks built from constructs, and a model would separate this synergy from standard technological or market-power synergies.

suggestions.direction: Test the outcomes directly by comparing completed deals with withdrawn or rumored ones (or using a matched set of non-acquired candidate targets), then measuring changes in complementor entry, integrations and multihoming after the deal.
suggestions.why: Saying the synergy benefits the ecosystem as a whole needs causal evidence on third-party outcomes, not only data on which targets were selected.

suggestions.direction: Rule out competing explanations (foreclosure, killer acquisitions, simple technological relatedness) and examine the welfare and antitrust implications for complementors.
suggestions.why: Linking the paper to live debates on platform and vertical mergers would broaden its relevance to the journal's economics and strategy readers.

revised_abstract: We study how ecosystem structure shapes acquisition choices and the value those acquisitions create. We propose a new acquisition synergy, ecosystem synergy: value that arises when combining the acquirer's and target's ecosystem positions improves alignment with third-party complementors. We develop a formal model in which acquirers choose targets to strengthen local interdependence, enter component clusters, or bridge them through centrality. The model yields predictions about which targets are chosen and how complementors respond. In e-commerce technology, we find that firms acquire targets that increase local interdependence among their components and their presence in component clusters. To move from target selection to value creation, we plan to compare completed acquisitions with withdrawn or rumored deals and with matched candidate targets. We will then estimate how deals change complementor entry, integrations and multihoming. We also plan to distinguish ecosystem synergy from foreclosure, killer-acquisition and technological-relatedness explanations. The analysis is intended to show when acquisitions in ecosystems create value for complementors rather than extract it, with implications for corporate strategy and merger policy.

what_we_value: We would value a computational model of how organizations search interdependent activity configurations and how that search is shaped by competitors, but we would ask what it adds to organization theory (search, learning, adaptation), and not just to strategy-as-economics, and how its mechanisms work at the level of the organization.

suggestions.direction: Recast the contribution in terms of behavioral search and organizational adaptation. Model local versus distant search as organizational processes driven by aspirations and performance feedback, so that competition alters the feedback firms learn from.
suggestions.why: Organization Science publishes simulation work, such as studies of experiential learning, temporal complexity, and political learning, when it builds on Carnegie-school theory of organizational learning rather than equilibrium competition.

suggestions.direction: Add organizational heterogeneity to the model, such as decentralized versus centralized search, cognitive representations, or inertia, and show how these conditions change the lock-in versus distant-search result.
suggestions.why: This would turn a market-level finding into organizational design implications, which the journal's community expects.

suggestions.direction: Add an empirical illustration that tests the disruption prediction, for example incumbents' configuration changes against entrants' positioning in an industry with measurable activity interdependence, such as app markets or video games.
suggestions.why: Linking the simulation's predictions to observable patterns would make the search-based theory of disruption more credible and better grounded in a real setting.

revised_abstract: Organizations search for configurations of interdependent activities while their competitors shape what that search finds. Yet theories of organizational search rarely treat competitors as part of the feedback that drives adaptation. We develop an agent-based model in which boundedly rational firms search NK landscapes through performance-feedback rules and compete in differentiated Cournot markets, so that a firm's position shapes both its internal fit and its distinctiveness. The model shows that under low complexity, competition reinforces local search and locks firms into their configurations, creating a trade-off between fit and distinctiveness. Under high complexity, competitive feedback triggers distant search, and fit and distinctiveness rise together. Competitive lock-in constrains early leaders, while distant search lets new leaders emerge, which offers a search-based account of disruption. We plan to extend the model with organizational differences in search structure and aspiration formation to examine when incumbents escape lock-in. We also plan to illustrate the predictions with longitudinal data on incumbents' and entrants' configuration changes. Our findings link behavioral theories of organizational learning with competitive dynamics.

what_we_value: SMJ would value a formal model that ties together two core strategy ideas, internal fit (NK search) and positional advantage (differentiated competition), and that yields a search-based account of disruption. Reviewers will ask whether the complexity-contingent results hold up under other modeling choices and whether the model produces predictions that can be tested.

suggestions.direction: Run robustness checks on the main mechanism: Bertrand vs. Cournot competition, different numbers of rivals, different ways of mapping configurations into product attributes, and imitation by rivals. Also show analytically or through decomposition why the result flips at a complexity threshold.
suggestions.why: SMJ reviewers of computational work (e.g., the benchmarking and behavioral real options models) expect the mechanism to be clearly isolated and shown not to depend on particular parameter or modeling choices.

suggestions.direction: State explicit, falsifiable propositions linking landscape complexity to how the fit–distinctiveness relationship changes and to which kinds of firms become leaders. Sketch an empirical illustration, for example product-attribute data from a modular versus an integral industry.
suggestions.why: SMJ rewards theory that the empirical community can test, and its formal papers increasingly point to measurable settings.

suggestions.direction: Position the disruption result against Christensen-style and capability-based explanations, and against the optimal distinctiveness and coherence/fit literatures (including dialectical views of incoherence). Spell out the managerial implications for incumbents choosing between local and distant search.
suggestions.why: A claim to have a new theory of disruption has to show what it adds beyond existing accounts in order to count as a contribution at SMJ.

revised_abstract: Firms seeking competitive advantage need both internal fit and a distinctive market position, yet strategy research says little about how the search for the two is related. We develop a model of strategic search that combines an NK landscape with differentiated oligopoly competition, so that a firm's resource configuration shapes both its internal fit and its distinctiveness. Under low complexity, competition constrains search: firms become locked into resource configurations and face a trade-off between fit and distinctiveness. Under high complexity, competition drives distant search, and fit and distinctiveness go hand in hand. Competitive lock-in constrains early leaders, while distant search drives the emergence of new leaders, which gives a search-based theory of market disruption. We plan to test the robustness of these results across modes of competition, numbers of rivals, attribute mappings, and rival imitation, and to decompose the mechanism behind the complexity threshold. We derive testable propositions about when incumbents are displaced and outline how they could be examined with product-attribute data. We contrast our account with capability-based and optimal-distinctiveness explanations of disruption.

what_we_value: Management Science would value a model that formally links search on an NK landscape with differentiated Cournot competition, but it would ask whether the results are analytically grounded and robust, or whether they are simulation artifacts tied to specific parameter choices, and whether the theory produces testable, falsifiable predictions.

suggestions.direction: Derive analytical results, such as the conditions for competitive lock-in and the complexity threshold, in a simplified tractable version of the model (for example, N=2 or block-separable interactions). Use the simulation to extend those results rather than to stand in for proofs.
suggestions.why: Management Science reviewers favor formal results with clear mechanisms over findings that come only from an agent-based simulation.

suggestions.direction: Benchmark the model's predictions against established models of disruption and entry, and run systematic robustness checks over demand, cost, and search-rule specifications (for example, Bertrand competition and learning-based local search).
suggestions.why: This shows that the fit–distinctiveness trade-off comes from the economics of competition, not from modeling conventions.

suggestions.direction: Add an empirical calibration or test, for example measuring product-configuration distance and leader turnover in an industry with rich data on product attributes, such as smartphones or automobiles.
suggestions.why: Pairing theory with evidence greatly strengthens a paper's contribution and audience at Management Science.

revised_abstract: Firms seeking competitive advantage need both internal fit and a distinctive market position, yet we know little about how searching for the two interacts. We develop a model that embeds NK-style interdependence among resource choices within differentiated Cournot competition, so that a firm's configuration shapes both its fit and its distinctiveness. In a tractable version of the model, we derive conditions under which competition locks firms into local configurations, creating a trade-off between fit and distinctiveness. We also characterize the complexity threshold above which competitive pressure instead triggers distant search, aligning fit and distinctiveness. Simulations extend these results to general interaction structures and test robustness to Bertrand competition, alternative demand systems, and different search rules. The model implies that competitive lock-in constrains early leaders while distant search allows new leaders to emerge, which yields a search-based theory of market disruption. We outline an empirical test that relates the distance between product configurations to leadership turnover in a setting with detailed attribute data. The analysis has implications for when firms should explore and for how competition policy views incumbency.

what_we_value: Organization Science would value a formal model that overturns an established result on optimal aspirations by showing that social versus absolute aspiration specification matters. It would ask whether the "simple" model reaches beyond individual bandit search to say something about organizing: how aspirations are set socially, who the comparison others are, and what happens when everyone in the population searches against everyone else.

suggestions.direction: Make social aspirations endogenous at the population level, so that peers' search changes the reference point. Model how strongly agents are coupled through rank or average targets, and how that affects the population's diversity in exploration.
suggestions.why: Organization Science values results that come from interaction among actors, such as ecologies of agents and competitive selection, more than results about isolated decision makers.

suggestions.direction: Spell out the organizational design levers. Compare who sets the targets (managers versus self-set), who the reference group is (inside versus outside the unit), and how many slots count as a 'top rank' in a tournament. Turn these into propositions about target setting and incentive design.
suggestions.why: Linking the model to concrete organizational practices would widen its audience beyond formal modelers and strengthen the 'implications for organizations' claim.

suggestions.direction: Add an empirical illustration or a calibration test, for example sales teams or R&D units that use relative performance targets in turbulent markets, or an experiment that varies the aspiration format.
suggestions.why: Organization Science often rewards models that generate testable predictions and show at least a plausibility check against real organizational data.

revised_abstract: Balancing exploration and exploitation is a central organizational challenge, and problemistic search triggered by unmet aspirations is a key driver of exploration. Prior models conclude that the optimal aspiration is lower in more turbulent environments. They assume aspirations are absolute, yet in organizations search is often triggered by falling short relative to peers. We develop an analytically tractable model of agents whose search is guided by social aspirations, either rank-based or average-based. We show that the optimal aspiration may instead rise with turbulence under rank-based aspirations, or stay constant under average-based aspirations. We extend the model so that reference points emerge endogenously from peers' search. This lets us examine how social coupling shapes how much exploration varies across a population and how well the population adapts collectively. We then derive propositions on organizational design levers: who sets targets, how reference groups are composed, and how tournament structures are designed. Finally, we outline a planned empirical illustration using units evaluated against relative targets in environments of differing turbulence. The analysis shows that the social structure of aspirations, not just their level, shapes organizational exploration.

what_we_value: SMJ would value a formal, tractable result that overturns a received finding on aspirations and turbulence, which fits its tradition of formal and computational behavioral strategy (e.g., the benchmarking and behavioral real options models). Reviewers would question whether "individuals' exploration" is linked clearly enough to firm-level strategy, competitive advantage, and managerial target-setting choices.

suggestions.direction: Recast the model at the firm or business-unit level, with rivals as the social reference group, so that rank-based aspirations become a matter of competitive positioning and performance heterogeneity across firms.
suggestions.why: SMJ rewards models that speak to why firms differ in performance, and relative aspirations among competing firms connect the result directly to competitive dynamics.

suggestions.direction: Treat the choice of aspiration specification (absolute, average-based, rank-based) as a design lever for managers, and derive conditions under which each one maximizes long-run performance, including mixed or hybrid targets.
suggestions.why: This turns an interesting analytical result into practical guidance on target setting and incentive design, which strategy readers would expect.

suggestions.direction: Derive testable propositions and outline how they could be checked, for example with tournament or ranking settings (sales contests, league tables, analyst rankings) where turbulence varies.
suggestions.why: Pairing formal results with a clear empirical route makes the contribution cumulative and easier for SMJ's largely empirical audience to take up.

revised_abstract: A central strategic challenge is balancing exploration and exploitation. When exploration is driven by problemistic search, how should managers set aspirations? Prior work finds that the optimal aspiration (the level that maximizes long-run performance) falls as environmental turbulence rises. That work assumes aspirations are set in absolute terms, yet firms and their units often search in response to falling short of rivals. We develop a simple, analytically tractable model of firms that compare themselves with competitors. We show that the optimal aspiration may instead rise with turbulence when aspirations are rank-based, or stay constant when they are based on the average of rivals. We then treat the way aspirations are specified as a managerial design choice. We set out the conditions under which absolute, average-based, rank-based, or hybrid targets perform best, and examine what these choices imply for performance differences across competing firms. Finally, we derive testable propositions and describe empirical settings with observable rankings and varying turbulence where these propositions could be tested. Our analysis informs target setting, incentive design, and behavioral theories of competitive search.

what_we_value: We value a tractable analytical model that overturns an established comparative static, here the claim that optimal aspirations fall as turbulence rises. We would ask whether the result holds once agents interact strategically and the aspiration is set by a principal, and whether it matters for real target-setting decisions beyond simulation-style behavioral theory.

suggestions.direction: Endogenize aspiration-setting as a design problem. A principal (manager) chooses the target specification (absolute, rank-based or average-based) and its level, and agents respond. Then characterize which specification is optimal as turbulence and population size vary.
suggestions.why: Management Science rewards prescriptive mechanism-design insights, such as optimal contracts, feedback and contest design, more than descriptive behavioral comparative statics.

suggestions.direction: Model the strategic interdependence created by relative aspirations. One agent's exploration shifts others' reference points, so the model should compare equilibrium with socially optimal exploration and connect the analysis to the tournament and contest literature.
suggestions.why: Relative targets create externalities across agents. Deriving their welfare and efficiency implications would link the paper to core Management Science work on contests and incentives.

suggestions.direction: Add an empirical test of the key prediction, for example using sales-force or online-contest data where targets are rank-based or absolute and turbulence varies exogenously.
suggestions.why: Management Science increasingly expects formal predictions to be paired with credible causal evidence, and recent papers on goal-ratcheting field experiments show this kind of pairing.

revised_abstract: Organizations rely on performance targets to trigger exploration, but many targets are relative: employees search when they fall behind peers rather than below an absolute benchmark. Prior work shows that the long-run optimal aspiration declines with environmental turbulence, assuming absolute aspirations. We develop an analytically tractable model in which a manager chooses both the specification of targets (absolute, rank-based or average-based) and their level, and agents engage in problemistic search. In contrast to prior results, we show that the optimal aspiration increases with turbulence under rank-based targets and is invariant to turbulence under average-based targets. We extend the model to capture strategic interdependence among agents, because one agent's exploration shifts others' reference points. We characterize when relative targets lead to too much or too little exploration compared with the organizational optimum, and which target specification a manager should adopt as turbulence and group size vary. We outline an empirical test using settings where target specifications differ and environmental volatility changes. The results inform target setting, incentive design and the management of exploration in organizations.

what_we_value: We value a simulation that moves attention from the knowledge being transferred to the knowledge it replaces, and that grounds resistance and sudden shifts in March-style mutual learning, but we would ask whether internal versus external fit gives us a new theory of hiring-based learning, with boundary conditions and testable propositions, or only a model result.

suggestions.direction: Turn the model results into formal propositions about which hiring firms benefit from which hires, comparing low-internal-fit firms with high-internal-fit ones, and set them against absorptive capacity and the learning-by-hiring literature.
suggestions.why: OS reviewers expect computational work to produce theory that others can test, not just to report model behavior.

suggestions.direction: Vary the organizational design: socialization speed, hire seniority or centrality, number and timing of hires, and turnover. Then show when the internal-fit advantage reverses.
suggestions.why: Boundary conditions grounded in design choices are what make the work matter to organization theorists and managers.

suggestions.direction: Add an empirical illustration that operationalizes internal fit, for example routine coherence in the inventor networks of firms that hire, or a field case of a firm absorbing a hired expert.
suggestions.why: A link to evidence would make the claim that resistance arises without cognitive or social constraints more believable to a broad OS readership.

revised_abstract: Organizations often hire to acquire new knowledge. Research on learning-by-hiring has examined the source, the recipient, and the knowledge being transferred, but it has largely overlooked the knowledge being replaced. We develop a computational model of mutual learning between individuals and organizations to examine how a hiring firm's existing knowledge, specifically its internal fit (coherence among practices) and external fit (match with the environment), shapes how it absorbs new knowledge. In the model, firms with lower internal fit absorb new knowledge more quickly, even when initial external fit is held constant. Mutual learning alone, with no social or cognitive constraints, produces both persistent resistance and sudden shifts. Extending the model, we vary socialization speed, the centrality and number of hires, and turnover to identify the conditions under which coherence becomes an asset rather than a barrier. We summarize the results as propositions about when hiring brings about organizational learning. We also outline a planned empirical illustration that measures internal fit through the coherence of inventor collaboration networks in firms that hire. The study reframes absorptive capacity as depending on what new knowledge must displace.

what_we_value: We value a formal model that recasts learning-by-hiring around the recipient's existing knowledge configuration (internal versus external fit), which ties into SMJ's work on fit, interdependence and imitation. We would question whether the counterintuitive result that low internal fit speeds learning has clear boundary conditions and strategic implications, or whether it is only a property of the simulation.

suggestions.direction: Turn the learning-speed result into a strategic trade-off. Model when low internal fit helps a firm adapt and when it hurts performance, and derive implications for which firms gain the most from hiring and how they should time it relative to environmental change.
suggestions.why: SMJ looks for contributions that speak to performance heterogeneity and managerial choice, not only to how fast learning happens.

suggestions.direction: Add strategic levers to the model, such as how many people are hired and when, where hires are placed in the firm's interdependence structure, and how integration is designed. Report how each lever interacts with internal fit.
suggestions.why: These levers turn the mechanisms into actionable propositions that link the model to strategic human capital research and to work on hiring for capabilities.

suggestions.direction: Tie the mechanisms to testable predictions and run a plausibility check against empirical evidence, for example learning-by-hiring through inventor mobility in patent data or executive hires that trigger repositioning.
suggestions.why: Pairing a formal model with an empirical illustration strengthens SMJ's assessment that the theory is credible and generalizes.

revised_abstract: Firms often hire to acquire new knowledge. Yet whether learning-by-hiring works may depend on the knowledge it replaces, which has received less attention than the characteristics of hires and recipient firms. We develop a computational model of mutual learning between individuals and organizations. In the model, a firm's pre-existing knowledge varies in its internal fit (coherence among practices) and its external fit (alignment with the environment). We show that firms with lower internal fit absorb new knowledge from hires more quickly, even when initial external fit is held constant. We also show that persistent resistance to new knowledge and sudden shifts can emerge from learning dynamics alone, without social or cognitive constraints. We then examine strategic levers, namely the number of hires, their timing, where they are placed in the interdependence structure, and how they are integrated, and we characterize the conditions under which faster absorption raises or lowers performance in stable and turbulent environments. Finally, we derive testable propositions and outline an empirical illustration using inventor mobility data. Together, these steps aim to clarify when hiring is an effective path to strategic renewal.

what_we_value: We would value a fresh angle on learning-by-hiring, namely the knowledge being replaced. But we would question whether an NK-style simulation alone, with no analytical results or empirical test, yields sharp and generalizable predictions. Most of our accepted work is either a tractable formal model or a well-identified empirical design, and pure agent-based simulations of organizational learning usually end up in the organization-theory and strategy journals.

suggestions.direction: Build a stylized analytical model, or derive formal propositions, that pins down when low internal fit speeds up absorption of hired knowledge, and use the simulation only to check robustness.
suggestions.why: Our theory papers stand out by delivering closed-form, counterintuitive comparative statics, not only patterns from simulation runs.

suggestions.direction: Test the core prediction with data, for example inventor mobility and patent citation data or a quasi-experiment such as a noncompete enforcement change, comparing how quickly hires' knowledge spreads in firms with more versus less internally coherent technology portfolios.
suggestions.why: Causal empirical evidence on learning-by-hiring would turn a simulation insight into a contribution our empirical strategy and innovation readers can build on.

suggestions.direction: Spell out the managerial levers: when to hire for knowledge, how many people to hire, and whether to restructure first to loosen internal fit, along with the performance cost of a temporary loss of fit.
suggestions.why: We expect clear implications for decisions firms actually make, beyond theoretical mechanisms.

revised_abstract: Firms often hire to acquire new knowledge, yet research on learning-by-hiring has looked at the source, the recipient, and the knowledge transferred, while largely ignoring the knowledge being replaced. We develop a formal model of mutual learning between individuals and organizations. In it, a firm's existing knowledge is described by its internal fit (how coherent its practices are with each other) and its external fit (how well they match the environment). We derive conditions under which firms with lower internal fit absorb hired knowledge faster, holding external fit constant. We also show that persistent resistance and sudden shifts can arise from learning dynamics alone, without social or cognitive frictions. Computational analyses examine how robust these results are across different levels of environmental complexity and hiring scale. We then plan to test the main prediction with inventor mobility and patent data, using changes in noncompete enforcement as a source of variation in hiring. We will compare how quickly hires' knowledge spreads within firms that differ in how coherent their technology portfolios are. Finally, we draw implications for when to hire, how many people to hire, and whether to restructure before hiring for knowledge.

what_we_value: We value how the study shows the tension between a social venture's legitimating narrative and its need to scale through stigma transfer, which links work on hybrid organizing and stigma, but we question whether a single-firm survey of purchase intentions builds enough organizational theory, beyond a marketing framing effect, to explain how ventures manage this tension.

suggestions.direction: Theorize origin stories as organizational identity claims that hybrid ventures use with different audiences, and build a framework for when stigma transfers to the organization and when it is diluted, drawing on stigma-dilution and category-straddling work.
suggestions.why: Organization Science publishes work that advances theory on hybrid organizing, stigma, and audiences, not demonstrations of a persuasion effect.

suggestions.direction: Add qualitative fieldwork inside the venture on how managers write, segment, or decouple origin stories across rural and urban markets, and add a second venture or product category with a different stigma.
suggestions.why: Process evidence and comparative variation would show organizational mechanisms and boundary conditions, and would address concerns about relying on one firm and one survey.

suggestions.direction: Measure actual behavior over time, such as purchases and the persistence of mailing-list engagement, and test the trade-off between purchase and support as a mission-versus-scale trade-off.
suggestions.why: Linking customer responses to sustained organizational outcomes would turn a hedged finding into a clear contribution to research on social–financial trade-offs.

revised_abstract: Hybrid organizations that scale beyond their original marginalized beneficiaries face a dilemma about identity. The narratives that legitimate their social mission may tie the organization to stigmatized groups in the eyes of new audiences. We theorize origin stories as identity claims that can transfer stigma from beneficiaries to the organization and its offerings. We also specify when framing around social responsibility turns that association into support rather than avoidance. We study this in an Indian feminine hygiene venture that is moving from rural to urban customers. In a survey-based field experiment, telling the origin story reduced urban customers' purchase intentions, consistent with stigma transfer. Framing the story around social responsibility increased non-purchase support. We plan to extend these results in three ways: (1) fieldwork on how managers construct and segment origin narratives across audiences; (2) a comparative experiment in a second venture whose stigma differs; and (3) longitudinal tracking of actual purchases and engagement. Together, these would show whether the trade-off persists. We contribute a theory of audience-contingent stigma transfer in hybrid organizing and show how mission narratives shape social–financial trade-offs during scaling.

what_we_value: SMJ would value a causal, field-based test of how a strategic-change tool (origin stories) shapes demand when ventures scale beyond their founding market, but would question whether an intention-based survey experiment with a single firm speaks to strategy theory (scaling, repositioning, value creation versus capture) rather than to consumer behavior.

suggestions.direction: Recast the contribution around strategy theory: frame origin stories as a repositioning and identity choice during scaling, and build on the optimal distinctiveness, stigma spillover, and market identity literatures to theorize a tradeoff between value creation (purchases) and stakeholder support.
suggestions.why: SMJ rewards papers that refine firm-level strategy theory, and right now the contribution reads as marketing or consumer psychology.

suggestions.direction: Measure actual behavior: run a field experiment using real purchases, conversion, or repeat-buying data, for example randomizing origin-story messaging across urban channels or ads, and track whether non-purchase support persists over time.
suggestions.why: Reviewers will discount purchase intentions, and observing behavior over time answers the open question of whether support is temporary or lasting.

suggestions.direction: Test boundary conditions and generalizability: vary how stigmatized the founding segment is, how visible the firm is, and the framing (social responsibility versus quality or capability), ideally across several social ventures or product categories.
suggestions.why: Showing contingencies turns a single-firm finding into a generalizable theory of when ventures should disclose or downplay their origins as they scale.

revised_abstract: Social ventures that scale beyond their founding marginalized customers face a strategic dilemma: should they foreground their origins or reposition? We theorize origin stories as a repositioning choice that trades off value creation in new segments against broader stakeholder support, through stigma transfer from the founding segment. In a survey-based field experiment with an Indian feminine hygiene venture that is expanding from rural to urban markets, origin stories reduced urban customers' purchase intentions, a pattern consistent with stigma transfer. When the story was framed around social responsibility, it increased non-purchase support. We extend this design with a planned randomized field intervention that measures actual purchases and the persistence of support over time.
