suggestions.why: Tying the practice to firm performance and to spillovers into the firm's capabilities moves the contribution from workplace safety to competitive advantage.

suggestions.direction: Test the mechanisms directly: separate incentive alignment from correcting shared misunderstandings, for example with treatment-arm variation or survey measures of manager-worker beliefs, and interpret the competition moderator through managerial slack versus attention.
suggestions.why: Identifying why collaboration works is what would make the finding generalize to other practices that need joint manager-worker adoption.

revised_abstract: Why do firms fail to adopt practices that would improve performance? We argue that many practices require joint effort from managers and workers, and that diverging incentives and inconsistent understanding between them create a coordination barrier to adoption. In a field experiment with 12,761 small and medium-sized firms, we encouraged owners/managers and workers to collaborate on workplace safety. The treatment increased safety training and reduced both the rate and the severity of accidents, without any increase in headcount. Our theory predicts, and our results show, that effects are stronger when managers are informed, when firms have intermediate prior levels of the practice, a narrow supervisory span of control, and low turnover, and when competition is weak. We plan further analyses that (a) use survey measures of beliefs to separate incentive alignment from the correction of misunderstandings, and (b) track administrative outcomes including productivity, survival, and the adoption of complementary practices. Together, these analyses aim to explain how manager-worker collaboration acts as a microfoundation of practice adoption and of performance differences across firms.

what_we_value: We value a large-scale field experiment that gives causal evidence on how management practices get adopted, a core Management Science topic, but we would question what the "collaboration" treatment actually manipulates and whether the heterogeneity analyses were planned in advance or found after the fact.

suggestions.direction: Build a simple formal model of manager–worker collaboration, with diverging incentives and asymmetric information about what the practice requires, and derive the moderators (manager knowledge, span of control, turnover, competition) as predictions before testing them.
suggestions.why: Management Science rewards empirical work that tests sharp predictions from theory, and a model would turn a list of heterogeneous effects into a clear mechanism.

suggestions.direction: Separate the mechanisms by comparing the collaboration arm with information-only and manager-only arms, or by using survey data on how well managers' and workers' beliefs line up, to show whether the effects come from fixing incentive conflicts or from correcting misunderstandings.
suggestions.why: Reviewers will ask whether this is a collaboration effect or simply an information or salience effect, and answering that is central to the contribution.

suggestions.direction: Quantify the economic returns using administrative cost data (insurance claims, lost workdays, productivity, survival), and test whether the effects persist and spill over to other practices.
suggestions.why: Showing net firm value and lasting effects connects the result to the management-practices and productivity literature this journal publishes.

revised_abstract: Many performance-enhancing workplace practices require collaboration between managers and workers to be adopted successfully. Diverging incentives and misunderstandings about what needs to be done often prevent that collaboration. We develop a model in which collaboration aligns information and incentives. The model predicts when collaboration matters most: it depends on manager knowledge, span of control, worker turnover and product-market competition. We test these predictions in a field experiment with 12,761 small and medium-sized firms that encouraged owners/managers and workers to collaborate on workplace safety. The treatment increases safety training and reduces both the rate and the severity of accidents, without any increase in headcount. The effects are stronger when managers are informed about safety, when firms have intermediate pre-existing safety practices, when supervisory spans are narrow, when turnover is low and when competition is weak. We plan further analyses to separate correcting misunderstandings from aligning incentives, to measure the cost savings and persistence of the effects, and to test for spillovers to other practices. Our results show that manager–worker collaboration, and the conditions it depends on, matter for adopting management practices and for firm performance.

what_we_value: We would value the clean natural experiment and the learning dynamics in how messages get used, but we would ask what the study tells us about organizing, learning, and how meaning gets constructed in exchange, beyond showing that cheap talk reduces bargaining breakdown in an economics framing.

suggestions.direction: Reframe the delayed effect as experiential and vicarious learning: test whether sellers learn from their own accepted or rejected messages and from their peers, and how they converge on a shared message repertoire, drawing on organizational learning and routines theory.
suggestions.why: Organization Science rewards contributions to learning theory, and the gap between adopting communication and getting results from it is a puzzle that learning theory can explain.

suggestions.direction: Theorize message content as relational and legitimating work (e.g., justification, warmth, signals of fairness), and code these categories to show which kinds of meaning-making reduce breakdown under incomplete information.
suggestions.why: The journal values mechanisms grounded in sociological and organizational theory, such as framing, trust, and relational work, more than an informational cheap-talk account.

suggestions.direction: Examine heterogeneity and boundary conditions, such as professional versus occasional sellers, seller reputation or status, and product uncertainty, and ask whether communication widens or narrows gaps between experienced and novice actors.
suggestions.why: Contingencies tied to experience and status speak to OS debates on learning asymmetries and stratification in markets and platforms.

revised_abstract: How do market actors learn to use new communication channels to resolve exchanges under incomplete information? We draw on organizational learning and relational perspectives on exchange to study how sellers develop messaging practices that reduce bargaining breakdown. On May 23, 2016, eBay Germany's Best Offer platform let desktop users, but not mobile users, attach free-text messages to offers. Using this natural experiment, a difference-in-differences design documents a 14% decrease in breakdown among compliers. Adoption was immediate, but the effect emerged gradually. Text analysis shows patterns consistent with repeat players learning, and messages that emulate experienced sellers' content are more likely to be accepted. We plan further analyses to separate experiential learning from vicarious learning, to code messages for relational and justificatory content, and to test whether gains differ by seller experience, reputation, and product uncertainty. The study aims to reconceptualize communication in markets as a learned, relational practice, and to show how platform design shapes who benefits from new means of meaning-making in exchange.

what_we_value: SMJ would value the clean natural experiment and the learning-by-doing evidence, but it would ask what this tells us about how firms create and capture value. As written, the paper reads as an economics or market-design study of consumer-to-consumer bargaining, not a contribution to strategy theory.

suggestions.direction: Recast the study around value creation and value capture. Break the outcome down into whether deals close (value created) and at what prices relative to list price (value captured), and show whether communication shifts surplus toward experienced sellers.
suggestions.why: SMJ readers judge contributions by how they inform theories of value creation and appropriation, and that literature lacks micro-level evidence on how communication is used in negotiation.

suggestions.direction: Focus on sellers that are businesses or high-volume operators. Test how heterogeneity among firms (experience, scale, reputation) moderates how quickly communication is learned and how much it pays off, and frame learning to communicate as a capability.
suggestions.why: Linking the delayed effect to organizational learning and to differences in firms' capabilities connects the paper to central SMJ conversations about learning, routines and competitive heterogeneity.

suggestions.direction: Use the text analysis to identify the specific bargaining strategies in messages (justification, signaling of reservation price, relational appeals). Test whether these strategies diffuse from experienced to novice sellers through imitation.
suggestions.why: Turning the text results into a theory of which communication strategies work, and how they spread, speaks to SMJ research on imitation, diffusion of practices and the microfoundations of strategy.

revised_abstract: How firms capture value in negotiations under incomplete information depends on whether they can communicate, and on whether they have learned to communicate effectively. We study this using a natural experiment. On May 23, 2016, eBay Germany's Best Offer platform let desktop users, but not mobile users, attach messages to offers. A difference-in-differences design shows a 14% decrease in bargaining breakdown among compliers. Although sellers adopted messaging immediately, the effect built up gradually. Text analysis shows that this pattern is consistent with repeat players learning to communicate, and messages that resemble those of experienced sellers are more likely to be accepted. Building on these findings, we plan three further analyses. First, we will separate value creation (deals that close) from value capture (prices relative to list price). Second, we will test whether seller experience and scale moderate how quickly communication becomes a capability. Third, we will classify message strategies and trace how they spread from experienced to novice sellers. Together, these analyses aim to contribute to research on negotiation as a source of value capture, on capabilities built through learning-by-doing, and on how firms imitate effective practices.

what_we_value: We value the clean natural experiment on a large platform and the text-based evidence on how communication operates, but we would ask whether the learning mechanism is properly identified, what the welfare and price effects are, and what this means for how platforms should be designed.

suggestions.direction: Separate learning from composition and selection effects. Use within-seller event studies by experience level, and compare how fast new and repeat sellers' message content converges toward that of experienced sellers.
suggestions.why: The paper's main claim is about learning-by-doing, so referees will want to see that the delayed effect is not just a change in who uses the feature.

suggestions.direction: Measure effects beyond breakdown. Look at agreed prices, the number of bargaining rounds, how surplus is split between buyers and sellers, and whether buyers return to the platform.
suggestions.why: Management Science readers care about efficiency and who gains, not only whether a deal is reached.

suggestions.direction: Turn the findings into platform design implications. For example, test whether suggested or templated messages modeled on experienced sellers could speed up learning, and frame cheap talk within the market-design literature.
suggestions.why: This links the empirical results to managerial and platform-design questions, which are central to this journal.

revised_abstract: Bargaining often breaks down when information is incomplete. We study whether allowing unstructured communication changes bargaining outcomes and how traders learn to use it. On May 23, 2016, eBay Germany's Best Offer platform let desktop users, but not mobile users, attach messages to offers. Using this natural experiment, a difference-in-differences design shows a 14% decrease in bargaining breakdown among compliers. Users adopted messaging immediately, but the effect appeared only gradually. Text analysis shows that these dynamics are consistent with repeat players learning to communicate, and messages that resemble the content of experienced sellers are more likely to be accepted. We plan within-seller event-study analyses to separate learning from changes in who uses the feature. We also plan to examine effects on agreed prices, bargaining length, and the split of surplus between buyers and sellers. Finally, we will discuss platform design levers, such as message templates based on experienced sellers' language, that could speed up learning. The findings inform the economics of cheap talk in bargaining and the design of negotiation features on digital marketplaces.

what_we_value: We value the clean field-experimental evidence on AI and entrepreneurial decision making, but we would ask what organizational theory explains why low performers are hurt — that is, which mechanism of advice-taking, problem framing, or learning is at work — rather than reading a heterogeneous treatment effect as the contribution.

suggestions.direction: Build a theory of advice selection and implementation that draws on organizational learning, the attention-based view, and absorptive capacity, explaining why baseline capability shapes which AI recommendations entrepreneurs act on.
suggestions.why: Organization Science rewards new mechanisms. Showing that people diverge in how they turn generic advice into action, rather than in what advice they receive, moves the paper from a policy evaluation to a contribution to theory on human-AI augmentation and learning.

suggestions.direction: Code the question-advice-implementation logs, and if possible run follow-up interviews, to describe how low and high performers frame problems, judge the fit of advice to their local context, and choose between substituting AI advice for their own judgment and complementing it.
suggestions.why: This journal values mixed methods that open the black box. Qualitative process evidence would ground the proposed mechanism much like recent Organization Science work on AI interrogation practices and artificial certainty.

suggestions.direction: Test planned moderators and boundary conditions, such as task type (generic vs. context-specific problems), entrepreneurs' local embeddedness and alternative advice sources, and whether advice cuts against or follows local practice.
suggestions.why: Specifying when AI advice helps or harms builds a contingency theory. That generalizes beyond Kenya and speaks to Organization Science debates on expertise, domain experience, and algorithmic advice.

revised_abstract: Generative AI promises low-cost expert advice, yet how decision makers turn generic advice into action is poorly understood. We develop a theory of advice implementation. It proposes that baseline capability shapes how entrepreneurs frame problems and judge whether AI recommendations fit their local context, which determines whether AI complements or replaces their judgment. We test this theory in a field experiment that randomized Kenyan entrepreneurs' access to a GPT-4-powered business assistant. We cannot reject a null average effect on revenues and profits, but effects diverge by baseline performance: they are more than 0.20 standard deviations lower for initial low performers than for high performers. Low performers did nearly 10% worse with the assistant, while high performers may have gained over 15%. The questions entrepreneurs posed and the advice they received were similar across groups. What differed was which advice they implemented. We plan to code interaction logs and follow-up interviews to trace selection and implementation practices, and to test moderators such as problem specificity and local embeddedness. These analyses aim to show how AI augmentation can widen performance gaps through how organizations learn from advice.

what_we_value: SMJ would value a randomized field test of AI as a source of strategic advice, much like its published peer-advice and AI-as-training-partner studies. However, it would ask whether the heterogeneity result says anything new about how decision makers choose and implement strategy, as opposed to being a development-economics estimate of a null average effect.

suggestions.direction: Frame the study within the theory-based view, the literature on entrepreneurial learning and experimentation, and the attention-based view. Theorize how low and high performers differ in their ability to screen, adapt and implement generic advice, and pre-specify mechanisms.
suggestions.why: SMJ rewards a clear theoretical mechanism. Linking the implementation-selection result to the strategist's cognition and capabilities turns a heterogeneous treatment effect into a contribution on the microfoundations of strategy.

suggestions.direction: Code the advice that was implemented by type: cost-cutting versus growth, and generic versus context-specific. Test whether low performers choose riskier or less well-fitting actions, and whether those choices depend on fit with the firm's existing resources and activity system.
suggestions.why: This shows why AI advice creates or destroys value and connects to SMJ work on fit, interdependence and imitation.

suggestions.direction: Present the findings as an AI-driven widening of performance gaps, where complementary capabilities determine who gains. Discuss what this means for competitive advantage when an advisory input becomes cheap and widely available.
suggestions.why: The journal cares about where firm heterogeneity and sustained advantage come from. Showing that a resource anyone can access widens gaps through complementary capabilities speaks directly to that concern.

revised_abstract: When strategic advice becomes cheap and available to everyone through generative AI, does it level performance across firms or widen the gaps between them? We draw on the theory-based view and on research about complementary capabilities to argue that the value of AI advice depends on whether entrepreneurs can screen and implement it in ways that fit their business. In a field experiment with Kenyan entrepreneurs, we randomized access to a GPT-4-powered business assistant. We cannot reject a null average effect on revenues and profits. However, the effect for entrepreneurs who were low performing at baseline is more than 0.20 standard deviations lower than for initial high performers. In subsample estimates, low performers did nearly 10% worse with the assistant, while high performers may have gained more than 15%. The divergence does not appear to come from differences in the questions entrepreneurs asked or the advice they received. Instead, it reflects which advice they chose to implement. In planned analyses, we will code the implemented actions by type and by fit with each firm's resources to identify how selection drives the gap. We discuss what these results imply for competitive advantage when advice is a widely available resource.

what_we_value: We value the causal evidence from a randomized field experiment on generative AI in entrepreneurial decision making, and the heterogeneity that runs against the usual "AI levels the playing field" result; we would question whether splitting the sample by baseline performance was preregistered, and how tightly the implementation-selection mechanism is identified.

suggestions.direction: Build a simple model of how entrepreneurs choose which advice to act on. In it, entrepreneurs differ in how well they can judge whether a piece of advice fits their business. Derive testable predictions from it and check them using the logs of the AI conversations.
suggestions.why: Management Science rewards papers that pair a formal mechanism with field evidence, and a model would turn a heterogeneity finding into a theory of how people screen advice.

suggestions.direction: Classify the AI's advice and the actions entrepreneurs took into types, such as cost cutting versus demand generation, or generic versus tailored to the business. Use this to show whether low performers picked riskier or worse-fitting advice. Address multiple-hypothesis testing, and state clearly which heterogeneity analyses were preregistered.
suggestions.why: Ruling out alternative explanations and pinning down the mechanism is what will persuade reviewers that the asymmetric effect is real and not an artifact of the sample split.

suggestions.direction: Compare the AI assistant directly with human mentorship or training benchmarks, or add a planned arm that offers curated or filtered advice. Tie the implications to the literatures on management practices and advice-giving.
suggestions.why: Placing generative AI next to established interventions makes the managerial and policy value clear, which fits the journal's focus on organizational design and entrepreneurship.

revised_abstract: Low-cost assistants based on generative AI could widen access to business advice in emerging markets. But because running a business involves open-ended problems, it is unclear who benefits. In a field experiment with Kenyan entrepreneurs, we randomized access to a GPT-4-powered business assistant. We cannot reject a null average effect on revenues and profits. However, the treatment effect for entrepreneurs who were low performers at baseline is more than 0.20 standard deviations lower than for high performers. Low performers did nearly 10% worse with access to the assistant, while high performers may have gained more than 15%. The questions entrepreneurs asked and the advice the AI gave look similar across the two groups, which points to differences in which advice entrepreneurs chose to implement. We develop a model of advice selection in which entrepreneurs differ in their ability to judge whether advice fits their business. In planned analyses, we use the conversation logs to code advice and implementation by type and test the model's predictions. We discuss what this implies for designing AI advisory tools and for theories of entrepreneurial learning.

what_we_value: Organization Science would value the firm-level text-based measure of competitive overlap, but it would question whether the paper says anything about organizations as such: as framed, the study reads as an economics or strategy test of competition and innovation (closer to SMJ or Management Science) and gives no organizational mechanism, such as attention, search, structure or the reallocation of people, to explain why firms innovate.

suggestions.direction: Theorize and test the organizational mechanism that turns competitive threat into innovation, using threat-rigidity and the behavioral theory of the firm. One example is reallocating inventors and teams from threatened to new technology areas, which can be traced in patent inventor data.
suggestions.why: Organization Science rewards papers that open the black box of how organizations respond, not just whether outcomes shift.

suggestions.direction: Explain why firms respond differently to the same threat by examining organizational moderators: slack, how decentralized R&D is, top management team composition, and whether the firm's identity is anchored in its product category.
suggestions.why: Asking which organizations respond with innovation rather than retrenchment is a core question in organization theory.

suggestions.direction: Look beyond patent counts at internal reorganization: how inventor teams are recombined, whether inventors leave, and how diversification changes the firm's internal structure. If feasible, add qualitative evidence such as 10-K narratives of strategic reorientation.
suggestions.why: This would link the findings to OS conversations on organizational adaptation, recombination and boundary change rather than only to methods.

revised_abstract: How do organizations adapt when foreign rivals suddenly encroach on their product markets? Drawing on the behavioral theory of the firm and threat-rigidity perspectives, we theorize that competitive threat triggers problemistic search, which reallocates organizational attention and inventive labor toward new technological domains. We measure each firm's exposure using text similarity between U.S. firms' product descriptions and those of Chinese importers in electronic and electrical appliances. Using a continuous difference-in-differences design, we find that more exposed incumbents increase their quality-weighted patenting and new-product patents and diversify into new technological and business segments. To unpack the mechanism, we plan to trace inventor reallocation and team recombination across technology areas with patent inventor data. We will also examine how organizational slack, R&D decentralization and the firm's product-category identity shape whether firms respond by renewing or by retrenching. Planned analyses of strategic narratives in 10-K filings will document how firms reframe themselves under threat. The study reframes import competition as an organizational adaptation problem and explains why similar threats lead to different outcomes across firms.

what_we_value: SMJ would value firm-level, text-based measurement of competitive pressure and the link to strategic responses like diversification. It would question whether the paper adds strategy theory beyond the well-established economics finding that the "China shock" affects innovation (Autor et al., Bloom et al.), and whether "initial Chinese market entry" gives clean identification.

suggestions.direction: Explain why incumbents respond differently using a strategy mechanism, such as resource redeployment, capability fungibility or competitive repositioning, and test moderators like slack resources, technological distance from the rivals and vertical scope.
suggestions.why: SMJ publishes work on why firms respond differently to the same competitive shock, not average effects that the economics literature already documents.

suggestions.direction: Link the innovation responses to outcomes: product-market repositioning, exits from contested segments, survival and profitability, and separate escaping competition from neck-and-neck innovation.
suggestions.why: Tying innovation to value capture and competitive advantage turns a descriptive result into a contribution to strategy.

suggestions.direction: Strengthen identification with instruments based on Chinese export supply to other countries, or with tariff changes such as the granting of PNTR (permanent normal trade relations), and validate the text-similarity measure against known competitor sets.
suggestions.why: Reviewers will expect exogenous variation in rivalry and a validated measure before they accept the methodological contribution.

revised_abstract: Why do some incumbents answer intensified product-market rivalry with strategic renewal while others retrench? We study U.S. electronics and electrical appliance firms facing Chinese import competition. To measure firm-level competitive pressure, we compute text-based similarity between each U.S. firm's product descriptions and those of Chinese importers, and we validate the measure against known competitor sets. Drawing on resource-redeployment and repositioning perspectives, we theorize that firms with fungible technological resources and slack escape rivalry by innovating into new segments, while constrained firms remain in contested markets. Using a continuous difference-in-differences design, we estimate effects on quality-weighted patenting, new-product patents and technological diversification. Planned analyses will add identification based on Chinese exports to other countries and on tariff changes. We will also test moderators: resource fungibility, slack and technological distance from the rivals. Initial estimates suggest that more exposed firms increase quality-weighted and new-product patenting and diversify. Planned analyses will trace the consequences for product repositioning, segment exit, survival and profitability. The study aims to explain differences in how incumbents respond to rivalry, and it offers strategy scholars a validated text-based measure of competition.

what_we_value: Management Science would value a credible firm-level measure of import rivalry tied to innovation, but would ask what this adds to the large China-shock-and-innovation literature (Autor et al., Bloom et al.), whether text similarity is exogenous to firms' own innovation choices, and what mechanism separates the competing theories.

suggestions.direction: Address endogeneity in the text-similarity exposure. Build the measure from pre-period product descriptions only, and instrument it with Chinese supply-side shocks such as productivity changes, tariff changes after PNTR, or Chinese exports to other rich countries, interacted with each firm's baseline product position.
suggestions.why: Firms that innovate may reposition their product descriptions, so reviewers here will expect the identification to separate competitive pressure from the firm's own strategic choices.

suggestions.direction: Write a simple model that predicts when rivalry raises versus lowers innovation, for example escape-competition versus Schumpeterian effects depending on a firm's distance to the frontier, financial slack, or how easily it can redeploy assets. Then test the heterogeneous predictions it generates.
suggestions.why: This journal rewards papers that settle a theoretical tension through sharp mechanism tests, not papers that only report average effects.

suggestions.direction: Extend the sample beyond one industry and link innovation to product-portfolio and performance outcomes: new product introductions, segment exits, and changes in profitability or survival. Also validate the text measure against benchmarks such as import penetration and human-coded rivalry.
suggestions.why: External validity and evidence on whether the innovation response actually pays off would turn a measurement exercise into a contribution on strategy and the economics of innovation.

revised_abstract: Does import competition spur or stifle incumbent innovation? We build a firm-level measure of product-market rivalry from the textual similarity between U.S. firms' pre-period product descriptions and the products of Chinese exporters entering U.S. markets. We validate it against import penetration and alternative rivalry benchmarks. A simple model predicts that rivalry raises innovation for firms near the technological frontier or with redeployable resources (escape competition) and lowers it for laggards. To identify effects, we plan to interact baseline product overlap with Chinese supply-side shocks, namely productivity growth, PNTR-induced tariff uncertainty, and Chinese exports to other high-income markets, in a continuous difference-in-differences design across manufacturing industries. In initial evidence from electronics, more exposed incumbents increase quality-weighted patenting and new-product patents and diversify into new technological segments. Planned analyses test the model's heterogeneity predictions and trace how innovation responses translate into product introductions, segment exits, profitability, and survival. The results speak to how firms strategically reposition under globalization, and the method offers a scalable way to measure rivalry for each firm individually.
